The AQ25742B is a zoning panel from Resideo (Honeywell Home).

A zoning control is what lets one boiler serve rooms that do not all want heat at the same time. Each zone gets its own thermostat and its own valve or pump; the panel takes the calls, drives the valves, and starts the boiler and circulator only when something actually needs heat.

The part that matters on installation is what the panel expects from the valve. A 2-wire valve is simply driven open; a 4-wire valve has an end switch that reports back when it has finished opening, and the panel waits for that before starting the circulator. Matching the panel to the valve type is what keeps the pump from running against a closed zone.

This panel is built for 2-wire zone valves.

Size the panel to the zone count you will have, not the count you have today. Adding a zone later means replacing the panel, and the cost difference between four zones and six at the time of install is small compared with doing it twice.

The AT140B1206 is a control transformer from Resideo (Honeywell Home), 140 VA, 120 V primary, foot mount.

Almost every heating and cooling control runs on 24 volts, and the transformer is what makes it. It takes line voltage in and delivers the low-voltage supply that the thermostat, the zone valves, the relays and the gas valve all share.

Size it by VA, not by voltage. VA is the load the transformer can carry, and every device on the control circuit adds to it — a zone valve pulls current while it drives, a relay coil holds current the whole time it is energized, and a Wi-Fi thermostat draws continuously. A transformer sized for the original equipment will not carry the same system after two zones and a smart stat have been added, and the symptom is intermittent: things work alone and fail together.

Mounting matters more than it looks. The transformer has to land where the enclosure has room and where the leads reach, and a foot-mount body will not sit in a knockout that was made for a plate mount.

Leadwires are 9 inches.

The Q313A1139 is a 750 mV thermopile from Resideo (Honeywell Home), 35 inches long.

A thermopile is a stack of thermocouples wired in series. Where a single thermocouple makes about 30 millivolts — just enough to hold a pilot safety valve open — a thermopile makes around 750, which is enough to run the whole control circuit.

That is what a millivolt system is: a gas appliance that needs no electrical supply at all. The pilot flame generates the power, the thermostat switches it, and the gas valve opens. The appliance keeps working through a power cut, which is why millivolt controls are still specified on fireplaces, wall heaters and standing-pilot unit heaters.

A thermopile that has aged puts out less voltage before it puts out none. The symptom is an appliance that lights and runs but drops out when the thermostat calls, or one that will not restart once it has cooled — the output is enough to hold the pilot but not enough to pull in the main valve.

Supplied with a push-in clip for the pilot bracket.

Thermopiles power the control circuit, so they pair with millivolt thermostats such as the T827K1009.
